deep.reconstruction:
Context: Tractatus de numerorum doctrina, Ch. XVI, 'On the divisors of numbers of the form xx+2yy'. Sections 571-576 (previous page) found that primitive values of x^2+2y^2 are ≡1,3 (mod 8) or twice such numbers, and proved the composition identity (aa+2bb)(cc+2dd)=(ac±2bd)^2+2(ad∓bc)^2. Section 577 begins the theorem: if N=a^2+2b^2 divides p^2+2q^2, then the quotient also has the form x^2+2y^2.

§577 (end). Assume a and b are prime to N. Then a and b are invertible mod N, so every residue class can be written as a multiple of a, and also as a multiple of b. Hence one can write p = mN ± f a and q = nN ± g b, in infinitely many ways. Then p^2+2q^2 ≡ f^2a^2+2g^2b^2 (mod N), so N | f^2a^2+2g^2b^2.

§578. Grant for now that the solutions always come from g = ±f. That is, take p = mN ± f a and q = nN ± f b. Expanding and dividing by N gives
(p^2+2q^2)/N = m^2N ± 2mfa + 2n^2N ± 4nfb + f^2.
This equals (f ± ma ± 2nb)^2 + 2(mb ∓ na)^2. [Check, mine: the cross terms ±4mnab cancel, and m^2(a^2+2b^2)+2n^2(a^2+2b^2) is recovered.] So the quotient is of the form x^2+2y^2.

§579. Justification of the assumption. Let 1, α, β, γ, … be the quadratic residues mod N. Since a^2 ≡ -2b^2 (mod N), -2b^2 is a residue. Hence -2 is a residue (implicitly: divide by the residue b^2). Hence -2α, -2β, … are residues: the residues are closed under multiplication by -2.

§580. For any q, choose g with q ≡ ±gb (b invertible). Then q^2 ≡ g^2b^2 and 2q^2 ≡ 2g^2b^2. Since N | p^2+2q^2, we get p^2 ≡ -2g^2b^2 ≡ a^2g^2 (mod N). So p^2 and (ag)^2 leave the same residue, and Euler concludes p = mN ± ag, i.e. f = ±g.

§581. Euler himself rejects this step unless N is prime. If N is prime, then N divides both f^2a^2+2g^2b^2 and g^2a^2+2g^2b^2. Subtracting, N | (f^2-g^2)a^2, so N | f-g or N | f+g. Since f, g are only defined mod N, one may take g = ±f. For composite N, f-g could be divisible by one factor and f+g by another, so the conclusion fails. Thus §§577-580 really prove: if a PRIME N = a^2+2b^2 divides p^2+2q^2, the quotient is again of the form x^2+2y^2.

§582-584 (descent bookkeeping, the analogue of Euler's 1758 two-squares proof). Let A, B, C, D, … be primes of the form x^2+2y^2. Divide p^2+2q^2 successively by such primes; each quotient stays of the form, by §578 applied repeatedly. So if p^2+2q^2 = (product of such primes)·𝔄, then 𝔄 is of the form. Contrapositive: if p^2+2q^2 has a divisor 𝔄 not of the form, the cofactor is not a product of primes of the form. If prime, it is not of the form; if composite, it has at least one prime factor not of the form.

§585. Let 𝔄, 𝔅, ℭ, 𝔇, … be the primes excluded from the form. Then p^2+2q^2 cannot equal A𝔄, AB𝔄, ABC𝔄, …. So among its prime factors there are either no excluded primes or at least two. The next page (§§586-587) finishes with a size/descent argument: one may take p, q < 𝔄/2, so the quotient is < (3/4)𝔄 and contains a smaller excluded prime divisor, giving infinite descent.

Marginal note 1. Hence p^2+2q^2 (p, q coprime) has no prime divisors ≡5,7 (mod 8), since by §575 those are not of the form. Consequently, for primes p ≡ 5,7 (mod 8), -2 is a quadratic non-residue.

Marginal note 2 (general n). If N = a^2+nb^2 divides x^2+ny^2, then N divides b^2x^2-a^2y^2 and a^2x^2-n^2b^2y^2. These follow from b^2(x^2+ny^2)-y^2N and a^2(x^2+ny^2)-ny^2N respectively. This is Euler's standard lemma: for prime N it gives bx ≡ ±ay.
errors: The core step of §580 (from p^2 ≡ (ag)^2 mod N infer p ≡ ±ag mod N) is invalid for composite N. Euler explicitly recognises this in §581 and restricts the argument to prime N, so it is a flagged gap, not a slip.
Hypothesis in §577 that a and b are prime to aa+2bb is not automatic. It needs gcd(a,b)=1 and a odd (if a is even, 2 | gcd(a,N)). It is stated as given rather than derived; harmless for odd primes N.
In §579 the inference that -2 is a residue from -2bb being a residue tacitly uses the multiplicativity of residues and invertibility of b mod N. This is correct but implicit.

§585's conclusion 'none or at least two excluded primes' is correct, but the repeated use of §578 tacitly assumes each successive quotient can again be fed into §577. It is fine since only prime divisors A, B, … of the form are removed. The final contradiction is supplied only on the next page (§587).
The marginal claim that -2 is a non-residue mod primes 8n+5, 8n+7 relies on the full divisor theorem (completed in §587), not merely on what is proved on this page.

results.what: If a prime N = a^2+2b^2 divides p^2+2q^2, then the quotient is of the form x^2+2y^2, with explicit formula (p^2+2q^2)/N = (f±ma±2nb)^2+2(mb∓na)^2 where p = mN±fa, q = nN±fb
results.modern_name: Division lemma for the norm form of Z[√-2] (prime of norm N divides norm => quotient is a norm); key step of Euler's descent
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (published versions, e.g. E256 'Specimen de usu observationum in mathesi pura', ~1759-61, and E164/E241 for the sum-of-two-squares analogue)

results.what: Recognition that the argument p^2 ≡ (ag)^2 => p ≡ ±ag fails for composite moduli
results.modern_name: Square roots modulo composite numbers (more than two square roots of a unit)

results.what: Descent framework: p^2+2q^2 with coprime p,q has either no prime factors outside the form or at least two; completed by size descent to show all prime divisors are of form x^2+2y^2
results.modern_name: Euler's descent proof that prime divisors of x^2+2y^2 are represented by x^2+2y^2 (class number one for discriminant -8)

results.what: -2 is a quadratic non-residue modulo primes ≡5,7 (mod 8)
results.modern_name: Part of the second supplementary law: (-2/p) = -1 for p ≡ 5,7 mod 8
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (observed/proved this half), full supplement by Lagrange/Gauss

results.what: If a^2+nb^2 | x^2+ny^2 then a^2+nb^2 | b^2x^2-a^2y^2 and a^2x^2-n^2b^2y^2
results.modern_name: Standard divisibility lemma for quadratic forms x^2+ny^2

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known descent treatment of divisors of x^2+2y^2, paralleling his published proofs (E241, E256). The Tractatus (E792) has been in print since 1849 and is discussed by Weil and others. Euler's own flagging of the composite-modulus gap is a nice detail but not new.
